articles.title_orig: Diplomacy or Transparency? Philippine Officials Consider Approach Amid Rising China Tension - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: Diplomacy or Transparency? Philippine Officials Consider Approach Amid Rising China Tension - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
Philippine Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi shake hands during a meeting in Manila, Philippines, July 22, 2026.
Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro announced on the last day of the 49th Summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) that provisional agreements have been reached with China on more than 80 percent of the text of the region’s draft Code of Conduct in the South China Sea, or COC. This means the Philippines ended its ASEAN chairmanship without finalizing the COC, which was designed to peacefully handle maritime differences.
But Lazaro was not just presiding over the COC negotiations and assisting President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in overseeing the ASEAN summit preparations. She also had to contend with serious criticisms about her work.
No less than the country’s ombudsman accused the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) of turning visa issuance in China into a business. The DFA denied this and called out the ombudsman for undermining its institutional integrity and maligning the reputation of foreign service personnel.
Meanwhile, human rights groups strongly denounced Lazaro’s recent high-profile visit to Myanmar to distribute aid in cooperation with junta-appointed agencies, and called it a legitimization of war criminals under the guise of humanitarian diplomacy.
But it was the escalatory war of words between some Philippine defense officials and the Chinese embassy in Manila over maritime disputes that grabbed headlines for weeks and forced Lazaro to intervene several times and remind Chinese diplomats not to erode mutual trust and confidence between the two countries.
The tension worsened to the point that it alarmed business and sectoral groups which released a public statement calling for de-escalation and the avoidance of “inflammatory rhetoric” that could further strain bilateral relations, including the promotion and protection of livelihoods and stable economic exchanges.
The DFA publicly endorsed the call and issued a separate statement about the “essence of statecraft,” and the supremacy of diplomacy in dealing with matters involving other countries. It did not mention names or offices, but the statement was clearly referring to defense officials who have been actively denouncing China’s narratives and actions related to the West Philippine Sea.
It asserted that civilian authorities should direct the country’s international relations and the importance of having a united stand. “In high-stakes diplomacy, a disciplined and coherent national voice remains essential to advancing our national interests,” it stated.
It highlighted that transparency is a tool but one that cannot substitute for strategy or statecraft. And it made sure that this point was clearly directed at the Philippine Coast Guard and other defense officials who have been regularly providing the public and the world with video evidence of China’s illegal activities in the country’s maritime territories.
“Releasing footage or shaping an online narrative does not, by itself, act as a physical deterrent at sea or a legal strategy,” the DFA said.
It added that the 2016 South China Sea Arbitral Award “was secured through rigorous legal proceedings under international law, not through public messaging or social media.”
It is mainly through diplomacy that the country negotiates disputes and formal protests. The DFA clarified that diplomatic engagement is not appeasement. “There are moments when public disclosure serves strategic purposes, and moments when discretion, restraint, and quiet engagement produce better results,” the DFA emphasized.
No defense official contradicted the DFA statement. But some political parties questioned why the DFA is reprimanding officials who have been exposing China’s illegal actions and harassment of fisherfolk. They expressed concern that aside from directing everyone to censor their views on the issue, the DFA’s stance appears to serve the interests of Beijing.
President Marcos’ spokesperson supported the DFA statement and called for unity ahead of the ASEAN Summit. At the same time, the official acknowledged that the statements and actions of defense officials are in line with their official duties.
What the DFA statement revealed was the internal differences in the Cabinet on adopting the best approach in addressing the rising tension with China. The country’s hosting duties for the ASEAN summit provided the DFA with the opportunity to aggressively put forward its views on the matter and receive the president’s backing.
Now that the summit has ended and the facilitation of the COC negotiations has been handed over to another ASEAN member state (Singapore), will the DFA retain the lead in promoting government discourse on issues involving China and the West Philippine Sea? Or will defense officials resume their active media engagement on China’s provocative maritime buildup and the necessity of strengthening military alliances, mainly with the United States and its allies, to serve as a deterrent?
If it finds itself sidelined by competing factions, the DFA should enjoin stakeholders to build a broader consensus on the value of making diplomacy work at all costs. More importantly, a citizen-led movement should amplify the call about what it really means to pursue an independent foreign policy.

articles.title_orig: 'Very good chance’ Nvidia knew of potential military use of its chips by China: FAI
articles.title_zh: 'Very good chance’ Nvidia knew of potential military use of its chips by China: FAI
articles.content_orig:
Washington — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that the administration needs answers from Nvidia as questions swirl about whether it has complied with export restrictions, after revelations surrounding its CEO's alleged affairs sent the chipmaker into crisis.
"We do need answers," Bessent said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
After Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO amid revelations about extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged spy, the U.S. is investigating how Nvidia may have given China access to advanced AI computer chips, despite government restrictions.
Last week, Bessent referenced a possible "culture of noncompliance" at Nvidia, questioning whether the company was "pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings." In an interview on Fox News, Bessent said he needed answers from Nvidia on its compliance with export restrictions within 10 days. On Sunday, he told Brennan the administration has not yet received those answers.
"We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers," Bessent said. "It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was."
Nvidia's CFO, Colette Kress, has taken the helm after Huang's departure. But Bessent has urged the company to bring someone in from the outside to run the company. The treasury secretary said Sunday, "We do need to see who was in charge of compliance there."
Asked how challenging it could be to get to the bottom of what Jensen Huang was doing, given reporting about Nvidia's "handshake" business approach, Bessent said, "For deals that size, there's no such thing as an untraceable handshake deal."
"There are bills ablating that movement, there are money movements," he said. "They may not be the 100-page documents, but it will be possible to understand what has gone on here."
On his call for an inquiry into whether Nvidia had a culture of noncompliance, Bessent said that it's simply a possibility that the dynamic was at play.
"We will see, and that's why I think the board is moving very quickly to establish whether this did or did not exist," Bessent said.
The comments come as President Trump has called for Jensen Huang to return as CEO of Nvidia. Asked whether the president understands the risks that Bessent has pointed to, Bessent replied that it remained to be seen "which level of the business knew about this."
"Was it at the lower levels? Was it at the middle levels? Did it go all the way to the top? And I have confidence that the Nvidia committees are moving very quickly on this and will come up with some very fulsome and robust answers," he said.
When pressed on whether he thinks it would be a good idea for Jensen Huang to return, Bessent said, "I think we have to see where the buck stops — Were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?" He also drew a distinction between this possible dynamic, and Jensen Huang's alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang .
"I think that is kind of a canard," Bessent said. "Was there a culture of compliance versus one person's foibles?"
Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee and will also be interviewed by House panels in early December.

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”

articles.title_orig: US Stock Futures Open Higher After Tech Selloff: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: US Stock Futures Open Higher After Tech Selloff: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures bounced on Sunday, as a shortened week on Wall Street got underway after all three major averages ended Friday in correction territory .
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 673 points, or 1.4%. S&P 500 futures added 2.03%, and Nasdaq-100 futures rose 2.76%.
In Asia, South Korea's Kospi fell 3.16%, with heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix down about 3.6% and 3.2%, respectively. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was marginally down. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index slipped 1.27% on its open, and mainland China's CSI 300 fell 0.58%. Japan's markets were closed for a public holiday.
Last week, major indexes tumbled as worries about the artificial intelligence trade continued to spook investors, despite Anthropic's record debut on Thursday.
By the end of the rout last week — which was the worst weekly decline for the Nasdaq Composite and Dow in more than six years, and the largest for the S&P 500 since April 2025 — all three of the major averages were in correction territory, and the Nasdaq turned negative for the year.
The Nasdaq-100 index ended Friday in bear market territory on an intraday basis, but was just shy of that mark based on the decline from its closing high on Oct. 6.
Investors this week will get a breather, no matter what price action looks like. Markets are closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday, and Friday's session will be shortened with the closing bell set to ring at 1:00 p.m.
All eyes are set to be on the shaky tech trade, as investors examine if last week's sell-off represented the market finding a durable bottom, or if equities have more room to fall.
Drew Pettit, chief investment strategist at Roundhill, said in an appearance on CNBC's " Closing Bell: Overtime " on Friday that the indiscriminate selling at the end of the week — which extended beyond just tech — is a sign the sell-off may be concluding. But, he said the burden of proof is on the bulls to undermine the bearish sentiment dominating the market.
"Fundamentally, I think the floor is a lot higher," he said about how low equities could go. "Technically… you need a string of catalysts for the bulls to prove the long-term earnings story isn't broken."
Asian markets kickstarted the week on a lower note, extending the sell-off from the previous week.
South Korea's Kospi fell 2.34% in early trading, while the small-cap Kosdaq was flat, with heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix down about 3% and 2%, respectively.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was 0.11% down.
Asia markets were set to open lower Monday, after a sharp sell-off last week as investors soured on AI plays.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 started the day down 0.49%, on pace for its eighth straight session of losses.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index futures indicated a lower open for the market, standing at 22,238 compared to the index's last close of 22,410.8. The HSI has posted losses for four straight sessions.
Japan's markets are closed for a public holiday.
Analyst Dan Ives said in a Sunday note to clients the panic in the market related to the artificial intelligence trades rivals other major sell-offs this decade.
"We are going through a tech sell-off that we would equate fear and anxiety wise with the March 2020 Covid days and April 2025 Liberation moments," he said, referring with the latter example to the market's reaction when President Donald Trump first introduced his global tariff scheme .
The Yorkville Ives & Co. partner and senior managing director warned there could be more room for stocks to fall, but he added the fundamentals of the AI trade are strong and that any downward movements will likely be temporary.
"This will be bumpy road over the coming months. That said, the technology age of AI is coming one way or another … and this is not going to slow down the 160 GW of backlog/demand power through 2029."
Despite the shortened trading week, there are still key companies that are set to deliver earnings over the period.
Two key hardware companies — Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Dell Technologies — will deliver their quarterly results on Monday and Tuesday, respectively, after the bell. Both have tumbled sharply this month, with HPE down 25% and Dell off 34%, amid the sell-off among companies with exposure to the artificial intelligence buildout.
Meanwhile, electronics retailer Best Buy is set to deliver results before the bell on Tuesday, while software company Workday will share its financials after hours on the same day.
U.S. equity futures jumped to begin trading Sunday evening, seeking to rebound from Friday's sell-off.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 412 points, or 0.8%. S&P 500 futures advanced 1.1%, while Nasdaq-100 futures rose 1.9%.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Has Lost $92 Billion and Nvidia's Board Does Not Intend to Bring Him Back. Here's What 9 Stocks Did the Year After Their Founder Handed Over - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Has Lost $92 Billion and Nvidia's Board Does Not Intend to Bring Him Back. Here's What 9 Stocks Did the Year After Their Founder Handed Over - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Jensen Huang has lost $92 billion on paper since Nvidia’s (NASDAQ: NVDA) record close on Oct. 6, and the board of the company he led for 33 years says it "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." In the 9 big founder handoffs that came before his, the stock beat the S&P 500 over the next year 4 times and trailed it 5 times.
Apple beat the market by 55 points in the year after Steve Jobs handed the company to Tim Cook. Microsoft trailed it by 43 points after Bill Gates handed over to Steve Ballmer.
If you are a long-time shareholder who owns Nvidia because of Huang, and the stock has grown into a large share of your retirement savings, that record is the closest guide you have to the years without him. Read as a forecast for Nvidia, it says the first year after a founder leaves is close to a coin flip; the limit on that reading is that none of those handoffs followed a scandal, and Nvidia’s did.
Nvidia’s board accepted Huang’s resignation on Nov. 11, and its chair, Harvey C. Jones, made the statement about reinstating him on Nov. 17. The stock closed Friday at $125.53, down from a record $239.24 on Oct. 6.
The figures come from 24/7 Wall St.’s new research report, "Nvidia Without Jensen," which used Nasdaq and New York Stock Exchange closing prices. Each line is the stock’s total return in the year after its founder stepped aside as chief executive, minus the S&P 500’s, in percentage points.
The gap between the best year and the worst is 98 points. Apple and Microsoft sit at the two ends of the list, and each had just seen a celebrated founder give up the top job.
Time helped. Three years after the handoff, 6 of the 9 stocks were ahead of the market. Starbucks and Nike trailed after one year and led after three.
My reading of that record: the business and the successor decided how those stocks did once the founder was gone, and the first year told you little about the third.
All but Apple’s were planned, and each company named its next chief executive when the founder stepped aside. Nvidia’s took four days from Huang’s note to his staff to the company’s announcement, and the board has not named a permanent successor. Here is the month in order. Press reports are marked as reports.
That leaves you with three open questions the earlier handoffs never carried: who will run Nvidia, what the board’s investigation will find, and what the SEC is examining.
Huang still owns 811.5 million Nvidia shares, according to his last Form 4 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission: 70.1 million in his own name and 741.4 million through family trusts and LLCs. At Friday’s close that stake was worth $101.9 billion, down from $194.1 billion at the Oct. 6 record. The difference is his $92 billion paper loss.
He can sell now. For three months after leaving he still counts as an insider, so large sales come with public notice.
Three things will tell you where this goes:
We’ll track all three in The Daily Profit, our free weekday email, starting with any large sales Huang reports over the next three months. Sign up free here .
My view, as analysis: expect the uncertainty to weigh on Nvidia’s price until the board names a successor and both inquiries are settled. The history gives you no reason to sell a great business only because its founder is gone. It also gives you no promise of a quick rebound, since most of those stocks trailed the market in their first year.
The bottom line: if Nvidia has grown into a large share of your savings, set the size of your position by how long you can wait. The record favored shareholders who could give a new chief executive three years.
Contact [email protected] for any questions or corrections.
I've been writing about stocks and personal finance for 20+ years. I believe all great companies are tech companies in the long run, and I invest accordingly.

articles.title_orig: Jim Beam won't resume distilling at flagship Kentucky distillery in 2027
articles.title_zh: Jim Beam won't resume distilling at flagship Kentucky distillery in 2027
articles.content_orig:
Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on Jim Beam’s decision to temporarily pause operations at its Kentucky distillery on America Reports.
Jim Beam will indefinitely pause production at its historic flagship distillery in Clermont, Kentucky, amid declining whiskey sales and record inventories.
The iconic American whiskey brand, owned by Japanese multinational brewing and distilling company Suntory Global Spirits , announced last December that it would pause production at its Clermont, Kentucky facility for one year, with plans to resume operations in 2027, Food Dive reported.
However, in a new development, it is now uncertain when the Clermont distillery will begin operations again, the company told The Courier Journal.
NEW 123.4-PROOF WHISKEY PROMPTS EXPERT WARNING THAT STRONGER ISN'T ALWAYS BETTER
Suntory told the outlet that it manages its Kentucky production in accordance with demand, inventory and long-term needs.
In December 2025, Jim Beam announced a one-year closure of its flagship distillery in Clermont, Kentucky, but announced last week that the facility will remain closed indefinitely as the company assesses production needs. (Noam Galai/Getty Images for NYCWFF and Bryan Woolston/Getty Images)
The company noted that it plans to reassess production needs in the future.
In the meantime, Jim Beam has moved production to its nearby Booker Noe Distillery in Boston, Kentucky, which, with an output of 45 million original proof gallons annually, is the brand’s largest distillery, according to Food Dive.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
The brand's Fred B. Noe distillery, located on the Clermont facility's campus, will continue its operations producing whiskey labels including Knob Creek, Little Book and Booker's, Inc. reported.
Fox News Digital reached out to Jim Beam and the brand’s parent company, Suntory Holdings, for comment.
Whiskey inventories are at record highs in the U.S. and Kentucky in particular as consumer demand for the spirit continues to decrease. (Bryan Woolston/Getty Images)
Jim Beam’s move comes amid an ongoing decrease in consumer demand for whiskey , with large quantities of the spirit sitting untouched.
Whiskey inventory in the U.S. is three times higher than estimated annual demand, global beverage alcohol data and insight firm IWSR reported in October.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"The unifying theme across Scotch, US, Japanese and Irish whiskey is polarisation by price tier: we are seeing growth narrowing to specific bands within each whisky sub-category, rather than spreading across the price ladder," said Marten Lodewijks, IWSR managing director and president.
Jim Beam's parent company said that it remains unclear when operations will resume at the historic James B. Beam Distilling Co. distillery in Clermont, Kentucky. (Joe Hendrickson/Getty Images)
"And in most cases, that growth is concentrating at the premium end, while the mainstream and value tiers absorb the pain," he added.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
Members of the Kentucky Distillers Association held an inventory of 16.1 million barrels of whiskey as of October 2025, according to the organization’s website.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Total beverage alcohol sales declined for the third consecutive year in 2025, according to IWSR.
Sadie Chafe is a writer on the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500 futures rebound sharply to rise 2%, kick-starting shortened week after tech rout: Live updates
articles.title_zh: S&P 500 futures rebound sharply to rise 2%, kick-starting shortened week after tech rout: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures bounced on Sunday, as a shortened week on Wall Street got underway after all three major averages ended Friday in correction territory .
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 673 points, or 1.4%. S&P 500 futures added 2.03%, and Nasdaq-100 futures rose 2.76%.
In Asia, South Korea's Kospi fell 3.16%, with heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix down about 3.6% and 3.2%, respectively. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was marginally down. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index slipped 1.27% on its open, and mainland China's CSI 300 fell 0.58%. Japan's markets were closed for a public holiday.
Last week, major indexes tumbled as worries about the artificial intelligence trade continued to spook investors, despite Anthropic's record debut on Thursday.
By the end of the rout last week — which was the worst weekly decline for the Nasdaq Composite and Dow in more than six years, and the largest for the S&P 500 since April 2025 — all three of the major averages were in correction territory, and the Nasdaq turned negative for the year.
The Nasdaq-100 index ended Friday in bear market territory on an intraday basis, but was just shy of that mark based on the decline from its closing high on Oct. 6.
Investors this week will get a breather, no matter what price action looks like. Markets are closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday, and Friday's session will be shortened with the closing bell set to ring at 1:00 p.m.
All eyes are set to be on the shaky tech trade, as investors examine if last week's sell-off represented the market finding a durable bottom, or if equities have more room to fall.
Drew Pettit, chief investment strategist at Roundhill, said in an appearance on CNBC's " Closing Bell: Overtime " on Friday that the indiscriminate selling at the end of the week — which extended beyond just tech — is a sign the sell-off may be concluding. But, he said the burden of proof is on the bulls to undermine the bearish sentiment dominating the market.
"Fundamentally, I think the floor is a lot higher," he said about how low equities could go. "Technically… you need a string of catalysts for the bulls to prove the long-term earnings story isn't broken."
Asian markets kickstarted the week on a lower note, extending the sell-off from the previous week.
South Korea's Kospi fell 2.34% in early trading, while the small-cap Kosdaq was flat, with heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix down about 3% and 2%, respectively.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was 0.11% down.
Asia markets were set to open lower Monday, after a sharp sell-off last week as investors soured on AI plays.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 started the day down 0.49%, on pace for its eighth straight session of losses.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index futures indicated a lower open for the market, standing at 22,238 compared to the index's last close of 22,410.8. The HSI has posted losses for four straight sessions.
Japan's markets are closed for a public holiday.
Analyst Dan Ives said in a Sunday note to clients the panic in the market related to the artificial intelligence trades rivals other major sell-offs this decade.
"We are going through a tech sell-off that we would equate fear and anxiety wise with the March 2020 Covid days and April 2025 Liberation moments," he said, referring with the latter example to the market's reaction when President Donald Trump first introduced his global tariff scheme .
The Yorkville Ives & Co. partner and senior managing director warned there could be more room for stocks to fall, but he added the fundamentals of the AI trade are strong and that any downward movements will likely be temporary.
"This will be bumpy road over the coming months. That said, the technology age of AI is coming one way or another … and this is not going to slow down the 160 GW of backlog/demand power through 2029."
Despite the shortened trading week, there are still key companies that are set to deliver earnings over the period.
Two key hardware companies — Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Dell Technologies — will deliver their quarterly results on Monday and Tuesday, respectively, after the bell. Both have tumbled sharply this month, with HPE down 25% and Dell off 34%, amid the sell-off among companies with exposure to the artificial intelligence buildout.
Meanwhile, electronics retailer Best Buy is set to deliver results before the bell on Tuesday, while software company Workday will share its financials after hours on the same day.
U.S. equity futures jumped to begin trading Sunday evening, seeking to rebound from Friday's sell-off.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 412 points, or 0.8%. S&P 500 futures advanced 1.1%, while Nasdaq-100 futures rose 1.9%.

articles.title_orig: Molly Meldrum: Australian music legend dies aged 83
articles.title_zh: Molly Meldrum: Australian music legend dies aged 83
articles.content_orig:
Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum has died aged 83 after a long illness.
The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.
Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars from King Charles to Elton John, who described Meldrum as the "single most important influence in Australian pop music".
In a statement, Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.
"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," the statement said.
Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.
Born in Victoria in 1943, he displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.
Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.
Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.
He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".
King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special , saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".
On Monday, Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon.
"One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music. A true champion of Australian talent, you will be missed, but never forgotten."

articles.title_orig: Automation system problem at Delta causes flight delays as Americans travel for Thanksgiving
articles.title_zh: Automation system problem at Delta causes flight delays as Americans travel for Thanksgiving
articles.content_orig:
Delta Air Lines has resolved an issue with its weight and balance system that caused nationwide delays leading into a busy Thanksgiving travel week, the airline said.
Calculating weight and balance on an aircraft is a critical part of the pre-departure preparations. Delta was forced to use “manual workarounds” on Sunday morning “to safely get flights departed,” the airline told CNN affiliate WSB-TV , as delays rippled across its network.
The system’s automation for departing flight weight and balance calculations is now working, Delta said. But passengers could still experience lingering effects from the holdup.
Over half of Delta’s total flights were delayed and 6% were canceled as of 9:30 p.m. ET on Sunday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware. Delta has said about 70% of Sunday’s schedule changes were due to the automation issue, which caused an hourslong ground delay at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport – Delta’s biggest travel hub and the busiest airport in the world .
The ground delay was canceled around 11:30 a.m. ET, according to an FAA advisory .
“Delta teams are focused on completing the remainder of today’s schedule. Cancellations, as always, are a last resort when all other options have been exhausted,” Delta told CNN, apologizing to customers for the delay in their travels.
Calculating weight and balance on an aircraft ensures the fully loaded aircraft is not too heavy to fly, is loaded properly and the pilots have the right settings for a safe takeoff.
Major airlines use sophisticated computer programs at their headquarters to calculate these numbers.
“Compliance with the weight and balance limits of any aircraft is critical to flight safety,” according to the FAA’s Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge .
For Delta, the weight and balance instructions for baggage crews are planned at the Operations and Customer Center in the Atlanta headquarters using a system called ALIS, or Automated Load Instruction System.
“Right now, it’s a system-wide outage for Delta Air Lines,” an employee explained to a pilot in Boston on Sunday morning in a radio call captured by ATC.com . “The ramp isn’t really able to load because there is no ramp worksheet in there, so that’s what we’re doing, we’re manually counting bags and doing a report for you guys.”
“Oh, geez,” the pilot responded.
“Kinda like the good old days across here,” the ramp worker noted sarcastically.
The Delta slowdowns come at the outset of what is projected to be a busy holiday travel period. Over four million travelers are expected at Delta’s Atlanta hub between November 19 and December 1, according to a news release from the airport.
Many travelers have already experienced long lines and frustrating disruptions in recent weeks after all flights nationwide were grounded just over a week ago, sparking flight delays and cancellations for several days.
The FAA has said the outages that triggered the nationwide ground stop likely stemmed from an outdated copper wire at a remote location.
Sunday’s Delta delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems, the FAA confirmed in a social media post .
The ground delay affected Delta flights and was not airport-wide, a spokesperson for Hartsfield-Jackson told CNN in a statement.
More than 60% of flights out of Hartsfield-Jackson were delayed Sunday evening, according to FlightAware, while around half of inbound flights to the airport were also delayed. The data does not specify how many of these delays were Delta flights.
Atlanta resident Shane Rocha and her family were traveling through Hartsfield-Jackson on Sunday morning to visit family, Rocha told CNN affiliate WANF. Rocha said she had flown earlier in the week without any issues and was hoping that today’s travel would be equally smooth.
“Luckily we’re only 19 minutes delayed, knock on wood,” she said. “Hopefully it stays that low.”
Although the specifics surrounding the Delta issue remain unclear, United Airlines experienced an issue with its weight and balance computer system in 2025 that triggered more than 1,000 delays and dozens of cancellations, the airline said at the time.
United also experienced a brief system outage on November 16 that affected fewer than 150 flights across the US, the airline told CNN. This outage appears unrelated to Sunday’s Delta automation issue and the previous nationwide FAA ground stop.
At the time of United’s outage, the FAA said the incident was not an agency equipment issue and the airline said there is no indication it was cybersecurity-related.
Beyond system disruptions, severe weather in the Northeastern United States has caused headaches as many people travel for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday.
Passengers flying to New York’s LaGuardia Airport and New Jersey’s Newark Liberty International Airport can expect around two hours of weather-related ground delays on average, according to FAA updates .
Weather has also sparked delays for flights to San Francisco, while San Diego and several Florida airports are experiencing departure hold-ups due to a high volume of flights.
This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title_orig: China Finds Another Route to Protein -This Time From Industrial Gas
articles.title_zh: China Finds Another Route to Protein -This Time From Industrial Gas
articles.content_orig:
China's search for new ways to produce protein is taking another interesting turn. Researchers at the Tianjin Institute of Industrial Biotechnology are investigating how industrial gases can be converted into nutrients for microorganisms capable of producing protein. It's another indication China isn't betting on a single technology to strengthen its future food supply.
The process begins with syngas — a mixture of gases that can be generated from industrial processes or biomass. Through fermentation, microorganisms convert these gases into compounds including acetate, which can then feed a second fermentation process. Chinese researchers have been testing how this nutrient-rich liquid can support the growth of Yarrowia lipolytica , a yeast with potential applications in microbial protein production.
The early results are encouraging. Researchers reported a 7.7% improvement in yeast biomass production in a five-litre fermenter, alongside an increase in acetate conversion from 21.68% to 41.1%. These are laboratory-scale results, not evidence that commercially competitive food protein is about to reach supermarket shelves. Nevertheless, they demonstrate another possible route towards producing useful biomass without relying exclusively on conventional crops or livestock.
What makes this particularly interesting is the wider Chinese strategy. From precision fermentation and cultivated proteins to microbial biomass and alternative fermentation feedstocks, Chinese researchers are exploring multiple approaches to protein production. Each has different technical and economic challenges, but collectively they could expand the country's future production options.
For countries such as New Zealand, the question is worth asking: if protein can increasingly be produced using industrial carbon streams, microorganisms and controlled fermentation systems, how might that change the economics of food production and national food security? China appears determined to find out.

articles.title_orig: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
articles.title_zh: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
articles.content_orig:
Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.
Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.
Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.
The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it s now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.
Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up in San Francisco.
Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.
But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn that this was a possibility.
Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).
What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?
One AI worker, employed by one of the largest companies in the city, is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.
He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.
But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"
Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".
Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.
"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."
If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.
That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.
One study found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.
But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.
For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.
"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.
Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".
Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.
Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.
Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.
"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.
Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.
But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism – which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness – are also growing, which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.
"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.
All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.
"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."
As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.
For Goldboss, the dog-walking company owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes – "always a reality in San Francisco" – she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she says.

Clint Henderson, managing editor at The Points Guy, explains why cruise costs are climbing and why sailing can still offer vacationers good value.
Cruise passengers are being warned they may need to provide extensive documentation for onshore activities at ports in Mexico.
The sweeping law now requires adults traveling to Mexico with minors to prove their relationship to the children in the group, or face denial of service at hotels, resorts and tours, the "Royal Caribbean Blog" reported.
Effective Nov. 14, 2026, an amendment to Mexico's General Tourism Law places pressure on tourism providers to verify family relationships, according to Travel Market Report .
CRUISE TIPPING CHARGES ARE 'OUT OF CONTROL' SAY PASSENGERS AS COMPANIES TOUT 'EXCEPTIONAL SERVICE'
The Mexican Senate unanimously passed the measure to combat child trafficking and exploitation, aiming to shed the country's status as a major destination for such crimes.
"Pedophiles don't come to Mexico by chance," noted Sen. Laura Esquivel Torres, as reported by the same blog.
A change to Mexico's General Tourism Law places pressure on tourism providers to verify family relationships. Pictured here, Carnival cruise passengers disembark at Costa Maya Cruise Port in Mexico. (iStock)
"Starting today, we will begin to shut down these opportunities," Torres added.
Fox News Digital reached out to Sen. Torres and Royal Caribbean for additional information.
POPULAR CRUISE LINE'S BIKINI CRACKDOWN COULD SURPRISE PASSENGERS AT ISLAND PORTS
Tourism operators are legally required to check documents and must notify authorities if an adult cannot prove legal guardianship or parentage, according to news outlet TravelHost.
Travelers should be prepared to present passports, long-form birth certificates and custody or guardianship paperwork, the same blog noted.
When cruisers in Mexico, pictured here, disembark at a port, they are required to bring documentation proving minors are related to parents. (iStock)
Documentation explaining any differing last names between a parent and child is also recommended.
Even if cruise passengers are only stopping in a Mexican port for the day, the rules apply to all local services.
11-NIGHT CARIBBEAN CRUISE ABRUPTLY CANCELED AFTER COAST GUARD DETAINS SHIP
While simply disembarking from a cruise ship might not trigger a document check, booking a beach club day pass, a local snorkeling excursion or renting a vacation home likely will, the blog reported (it is not affiliated with Royal Caribbean).
When walking around shops in Costa Maya, Mexico, families must bring documentation explaining differing last names between a parent and child. (iStock)
Travelers are urged to call hotels and tour operators in advance to confirm paperwork requirements.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
The Mexican government has not yet released an official checklist, but travel experts advise bringing a folder with these documents, according to the same blog:
Travelers have been taking to Reddit to weigh in on the new rules.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES
"This is going to be a mess," one person wrote.
"There has been no formal guidance given by the Mexican government on what will be accepted and different hotels (including different people at the same hotel) have been giving different answers," the same commenter added.
Royal Caribbean passengers disembarking from the Oasis of the Seas, pictured here, will require documentation for minors in Cozumel, Mexico. (iStock)
"Bring all government docs and letters from parent authorizing you to have [temporary] guardianship of their kids for travel," another Reddit user said. "Not that hard, really."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"I own a travel agency and [before that] was a Spanish teacher for 17 years. [I] traveled to Mexico with my students every summer and I always had a form for this — they used to often check," a third Reddit user said.
Cruise passengers on the Norwegian Joy cruise ship, pictured above, in Costa Maya, Mexico, will need documentation for minors. (Jeff Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
Another chimed in, "My only issue with using the birth [certificate] proof is that a passport and birth certificate are often the only, or certainly the two most important identity documents, a child has. Having both lost or stolen while out of the country would be very stressful to deal with."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"I also don’t understand why it matters for hotels," the Reddit user added.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Mexican Embassy in the United States, Mexico's Secretariat of Tourism and World Vision Mexico for more information.
Jessica Mekles is an editor on the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

The southern city of Odesa and surrounding areas have suffered "serious damage" to their main power grids following repeated Russian attacks on critical infrastructure, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo said on Nov. 22.
The electricity supply situation in Odesa Oblast is "extremely difficult" after key power infrastructure supplying households sustained "significant" damage. Repair crews are working to restore electricity, but continued Russian attacks and air raid alerts are disrupting their work, according to Ukrenergo.
"The situation is significantly complicated by constant threats of new attacks and air raid alerts, which prevent repair crews from always working continuously," the company said .
The situation in the Odesa area worsened following the large-scale Russian attack on Nov. 20, after which regional governor Oleh Kiper reported disruptions to the power grids.
The outages have disrupted daily life across the city. Schools in Odesa will switch to online classes for a week starting Nov. 23, local authorities said .
The power cuts have also forced the city to temporarily suspend electric public transportation, including trolleybuses. Local media have also reported disruptions to water and heating supplies.
The damage in Odesa comes as Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukrainian critical infrastructure across the country in recent months, targeting power grids, substations, and water supply facilities as the temperature continues to drop.
Ukraine faces an increasingly severe shortage of Patriot interceptor missiles that can counter ballistic threats, making it difficult for the country to defend itself from the intensifying attacks.
The power and water supply situation across Ukraine, including in Kyiv, has significantly worsened over November, with Russia launching its latest massive aerial assault with missiles and drones on Nov. 20.
The Energy Ministry said on Nov. 22 that Russia attacked an unspecified number of energy facilities over the past day, leaving households in central-eastern Dnipropetrovsk, western Zhytomyr, northeastern Kharkiv, and Odesa oblasts without power this morning.
Of these regions, Odesa Oblast faces the most difficult situation, the ministry said.
"The enemy is purposefully attacking energy facilities important for the region's power supply," the ministry said . "As a result, a significant number of consumers remain without power," it added, without elaborating on the number.
The utility workers managed to partially restore power to critical infrastructure facilities in the Odesa area this morning, and backup power schemes are currently being developed to restore electricity to the rest, according to Ukrenergo.
Asami Terajima is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent covering Ukrainian military affairs and front-line developments. She is the co-author of the weekly War Notes newsletter. She previously worked as a business reporter for the Kyiv Post, focusing on international trade, infrastructure, investment, and energy. Originally from Japan, Terajima moved to Ukraine during childhood and completed her bachelor's degree in Business Administration in the U.S. She is the winner of the Thomson Reuters Foundation's Kurt Schork Award in International Journalism 2023 (Local Reporter category) and the George Weidenfeld Prize, awarded as part of Germany's Axel Springer Prize 2023. She was also featured on the Media Development Foundation's 2023 "25 under 25: Young and Bold" list of emerging media makers in Ukraine. She is among the finalists for the U.K.'s One World Media Award 2026 in the Print category and the French Bayeux Calvados-Normandy award 2025 for war correspondents in the Young Reporter category.
Several people remain missing as rescue operations continue in Dymer, where a Russian drone destroyed part of a residential building on Nov. 22.
The plant is considered one of the important suppliers of petroleum products in southern Russia supplying the Russian armed forces.
In the newest announcement, the Lublin District Prosecutor’s Office revealed that debris from Kh-101 cruise missiles was discovered at three sites in eastern Poland: Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik, and Mołodycz.
A petition for Kim's resignation has garnered 25,605 signatures, requiring the Cabinet of Ministers to review and respond within 10 days.
"The enemy is deliberately terrorizing the civilian population, attacking civilian infrastructure, and taking lives," Governor Tymur Tkachenko said.
Libyan officials have reported that the Russian Navy corvette Merkury was severely damaged by Ukrainian sea drones. Kyiv has not commented on the claim.
The drills focused on small drones, including first-person-view (FPV) models, Ukraine's General Staff said.
Repair crews are working to restore electricity, but continued Russian attacks and air raid alerts are disrupting their work, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky again urged Washington to authorize the transfer of Patriot missiles that Ukraine's allies have already paid for.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russian troops launched 186 attack drones against Ukraine overnight, of which 161 were shot down.
The number includes 2,310 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
Ahead of the reported attack, a temporary ground stop was imposed at Krasnodar Airport, officials reported, amid the presence of drones in the nearby airspace.
Kyiv and London finalized an agreement on Nov. 21 that will see the United Kingdom manufacture "middle strike" and long-range drones for Ukraine on British soil, Ukraine's Defense Ministry announced.

articles.content_orig:
The charts say that we’re just about short-term oversold and ready to bounce. Let’s take a look at the indicators to see when that bounce might happen and whether it will last.
You've reached your free article limit
You've read 0 of 1 free Pro articles.
Everyone sees it. How can they not see that we’re just about short-term oversold? When the S&P falls seven straight days, even folks who don’t even understand the concept (or pretend not to!) know the market is short-term oversold.
As you know, I have been eyeing that midweek (Tuesday/Wednesday) time frame for us to get short-term oversold. That has not changed. Many of the charts came right to the top of their spring gaps. I would love to see those gaps filled on Monday. Will we get it? I do not know.
For example, there is that gap on the chart of the SOX at 8000 (nice round number) that I am certain even my mother could see (and no, she has not called yet). There is also that gap on the chart of the QQQs at 590.
That doesn’t mean there isn’t some support in the areas the market closed on Friday, just that oftentimes gaps beckon to be filled.
But as you know, I prefer the indicators. The VIX is jumpy. Can it get jumpier? For sure. Friday’s put/call ratio chimed in at 1.13, which was also the third straight day of readings over 1.0, so we have finally got some put buying going on. The ten-day moving average of the put/call ratio is now .96, just shy of that July peak. I would not be surprised to see this climb higher in the coming days, but I can no longer scoff that it isn’t high enough. It goes on the positive side of the ledger now.
The QQQs chimed in with some serious volume at 134 million shares. This is the highest volume since the Taper Tantrum. It is also the second time we’ve seen over 100 million shares traded during this rout.
The Nasdaq McClellan Summation Index, which I use volume instead of breadth for, has been in a downtrend for months. As of Friday, it needs a net differential of +15 billion shares (up minus down volume) to stop going down. That is the highest since March of 2021. It’s extreme.
The DSI for both Nasdaq and the S&P are now at 9. Can they go lower? Yes, but my experience is that once this gets to single digits—and my indicators are oversold—we are due for a bounce.
What we don’t have is any positive divergences, as the number of stocks making new lows expanded to extreme levels on Friday, with Nasdaq the most extreme, at nearly 1300 stocks making new lows. Down below you will see the Nasdaq Hi-Lo Indicator is back into oversold territory.
I still think this is a bear market, and I suspect rebounds will get sold. I do not think we have extreme fear yet (there has still not been a day where everything gets sold and 90% of the volume is on the downside), but we are oversold, and we have enough of the short-term indicators that say expect a rally this week.
I will always turn toward the indexes if I am looking for an oversold rally. This time is no different. I’d go with the SMH (SOX) or QQQs. If you prefer not to play for a rally, then you can look to do some selling into the rally.
The Hi-Lo is discussed above.
Helene welcomes your questions about Top Stocks and her charting strategy and techniques. Please send an email directly to Helene with your questions. However, please remember that TheStreet.com Top Stocks is not intended to provide personalized investment advice. Email Helene here .
Down below, you will see I have been asked about a number of technology stocks. The only thing I see that can change their negative chart patterns would be if we see a huge gap up Monday morning that holds, and many of these charts leave Friday’s action as an island down below.
Xeris ( XERS ) is a light among darkness and hasn’t done a thing wrong except get overbought (in a panicky market, this would have been down last week). I’d say a correction is probably on the table if it trades under 16.
CRH ( CRH ) had a nice rally to resistance, and I would expect a bounce from that 83-85 area, but I think charts like this need to build bases, and that takes a long time. So an oversold bounce from that support is the best I see for now.
Agnico Eagle Mines ( AEM ) curiously has not made a lower low along with gold. And the DSI for gold is now 9. I would look for a bounce from this 145-150 area. Resistance is light at 160 and much heavier at 170’s gap fill.
Micron ( MU ) is oversold, and support is far away at 450. Resistance is at 650 and stronger at 700. Because I think the semis rally, I would love to see this down one more day before a rebound. If it cannot recapture 700, then I think on a longer-term basis this will head back to the 450 area.
My old friend Western Digital ( WDC ) finds itself with some decent support in the 250 area. If that breaks badly, then the next support (and measured target) is all the way down at 175.
Sandisk ( SNDK ) is into support near 70. Unless it can gap up over 95 and hold it (leaving Friday’s action as an island), then I’d look for resistance in that 95-100 area.
Netflix ( NFLX ) is perhaps indicative of this bear market. A former fan favorite that keeps enjoying terrific rallies but in the end just goes on to make lower lows. It’s oversold and at some support, but a rally into the low to mid 60s is about the best I think it can do at this moment in time.
Nebius ( NBIS ) is oversold, at support, and due for a bounce. I don’t even know where I would put resistance except in that 110-115 area. The question is if it can get that far.

articles.title_orig: China's industrial strength benefits global growth
articles.title_zh: China's industrial strength benefits global growth
articles.content_orig:
By MA SI in Shenzhen, Guangdong | 
          China Daily |
          Updated: 2026-11-23 07:26
China's manufacturing prowess is not "stealing jobs" from the rest of the world but creating shared opportunities through localized production, technology transfers and complementary trade, business leaders and experts said.
They made the comments during the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders' Week in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, pushing back against the so-called "China Shock 2.0" narrative that portrays the country's industrial rise as a zero-sum threat to global employment.
Wang Chuanfu, chairman and president of Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD, said many people outside China have some misconceptions about the country's manufacturing capabilities.
Citing BYD's operations in Chile, Wang said the company purchases large quantities of copper and lithium there and supplies Chinese electric buses that help improve the local environment.
"Our trade is complementary," he said. "We not only export Chinese technology to the world but also bring jobs and tax revenue to local communities, achieving mutually beneficial cooperation and win-win outcomes."
He said that the company's plant in Thailand, with an annual production capacity of 150,000 new energy vehicles, employs nearly 6,000 workers, more than 95 percent of them Thai. He added that most components are sourced locally. Similar arrangements exist at BYD's plants in Indonesia and Brazil.
"We work with 12,000 suppliers globally and aim to benefit the world with Chinese technology through local procurement and research and development," Wang said.
Lei Jun, CEO and chairman of Xiaomi, said, "Asia-Pacific economies form the world's core industrial and supply chain region and the most promising consumer market with strong complementarity and cooperation potential despite their differences."
The company's cars and smartphones require thousands of components, which can only be completed through global supply chain collaboration, he said. "Xiaomi cars will officially enter overseas markets next year," Lei added.
Noting that the automotive industry is a pillar industry in many countries, Lei said cooperating with local supply chains will enable products to better serve local consumers. "We will maintain an open mindset and deepen cooperation with local enterprises," he said.
The European market, including Germany, is among Xiaomi cars' overseas destinations in 2027, and the automaker has already signed memorandums of understanding with eight leading German automotive dealer groups.
Wang Zhisheng, vice-president of the China Chamber of Commerce to the EU, said: "Chinese companies are well aware of the importance of localization — moving from selling cars to Europe to building cars in Europe. We are creating abundant job opportunities for local communities."
BYD's Hungarian plant is set to begin mass production in the fourth quarter of 2026.
Liu Jincheng, founder and chairman of EVE Energy, a major Chinese lithium battery maker, said reaching consensus and co-construction are key aspects of Chinese companies going global.
EVE Energy has built a lithium battery plant in Malaysia and begun nickel resource operations in Indonesia, with nickel already in use in large quantities in luxury cars such as BMW. Its full-industry-chain project in Indonesia will bring electricity to more islands and villages, Liu said.
Li Jiaying, an associate research fellow at Renmin University of China's Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies, said China's real economy is not a source of crisis, but a pillar of global stability.
Describing the so-called "China Shock 2.0" as a deliberately crafted political narrative, Li said that it represents a self-preservation strategy adopted by certain countries confronting industrial disadvantages and domestic deindustrialization. Such countries employ public opinion smears and trade barriers to divert attention from their internal pressures.
Jostein Hauge, a political economist at the University of Cambridge, said the "China Shock 2.0" narrative is steeped in double standards and hegemonic anxiety, while intentionally understating the vast benefits that China's integration into the global economy has delivered to the world.

articles.content_orig:
MONDAY PUZZLE — As Wordplay columnists, we don’t often share our feelings with the solving community. We don’t want to come on too strong, lest it scare off the newer faces. But there are three little words I haven’t said here in a while, and I need the new solvers to hear them: Start with Mondays.
Don’t worry. You don’t have to say it back. This is just a one-way tip for developing a solving habit without tearing your hair out. Monday puzzles tend to be the easiest of the week; the grids and clues get harder as the days go on. This doesn’t mean you won’t run into a few sticking points or have to look something up, but that’s why this column exists.
And who says you have to solve alone? You can always pull in a more experienced friend to show you how to approach a clue list or what to do when stuck. In fact, considering the theme of this crossword by Dena Verkuil, I might insist you make it a double.
The revealer at 59-Across asks for [Words from a bartender … or a hint to the ends of 16-, 26- and 48-Across]. “What’ll it be?” and “Why the long face?” come to mind.
Here’s what we get from the cited entries: The [1989 buddy cop comedy starring Tom Hanks alongside Beasley the Dog] at 16A is “TURNER AND HOOCH.” At 26A, the [Elusive ingredient for success] is SECRET SAUCE. And the [Titular role played by Michael Keaton in 1988 and 2024] at 48A is BEETLEJUICE. Hooch, sauce and juice are slang terms for noxious substances. So, go ahead, PICK YOUR POISON.
6A. Crossword clues often give idiomatic context to their entries. One tends to refer to [Societal woes], for instance, as ILLS. Societal “problems” or “evils” just doesn’t have the same ring to it.

articles.title_orig: Tech Snafus Have People Prepping for the Worst
articles.title_zh: Tech Snafus Have People Prepping for the Worst
articles.content_orig:
The number of Americans stockpiling bottled water, non-perishable food and other emergency supplies has spiked over the past few weeks, a trend that has only accelerated in the wake of a series of high-profile tech outages.
The jump in purchases has triggered questions to the highest levels of the administration, with both U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance trying to assure Americans there's no need for doomsday prepping.
"Tell them to relax, everything's good," Trump said in a Thursday interview with Fox News . "I'll let you know if there's a problem."
"A lot of my friends have reached out asking if they should prepare to build a bunker or stock up on food and water,” Vance told Fox News earlier this week. “My answer to that is no."
The evidence of stockpiling is far and wide, including U.S. media reports of recent spikes in sales of emergency supplies at stores in California, Ohio and Oklahoma .
Walmart customers were stocking up on more propane, bottled water and camping gear than usual earlier ​this month, a company spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday.
Trump officials grilled over tech outages that have Americans on edge
Survival Frog, an online U.S. retailer specializing in emergency supplies, says its sales volume shot up 450 per cent in the three weeks since Oct. 27, with new customers accounting for the bulk of the increase, Axios reported on Thursday.
Since late October, Costco's U.S. sales data showed an increase in purchases of "rice, canned goods, water, paper products, generators, batteries and similar items seemingly in response to a variety of concerns on social media," a company executive told Bloomberg this week.
Web searches for "emergency supplies" are up 300 per cent in the past month compared with the same time period last year, according to Google Trends.
The start of the stockpiling began several weeks before the recent string of tech failures .
It traces back to misleading TikTok and Facebook posts that followed a directive from Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth.
Originally announced in late September, the Pentagon initiative dubbed FORTRESS America (Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability) includes a plan for every major U.S. military installation to have the capability to generate its own electricity.
The start of the stockpiling began several weeks before the recent  string of tech failures. It traces back to misleading TikTok and Facebook posts that followed a directive from Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. (Leonardo Fernandez Viloria/Reuters)
"So bases remain lit, aircraft fly, and command centers stay online even if the civilian grid is taken down by cyberattack or sabotage," said the Pentagon news release on Hegseth's announcement.
On Oct. 25, Fox News reported more details of Hegseth's directive, including a specific nugget about a 90-day time frame.
"The Pentagon is preparing U.S. military bases to keep operating for at least 90 days without outside support as it prepares for the possibility of a major war that could cripple power grids, disrupt supply chains and threaten critical infrastructure on American soil," said the report.
Within days of that story, Google searches for "90 day power outage" spiked by 5,000 per cent and retailers saw jumps in customers buying emergency supplies.
Videos quickly mushroomed on TikTok and YouTube twisting the content of the Fox News story, either suggesting that the U.S. government was warning people to prepare for a 90-day blackout or that the government was itself preparing for a 90-day blackout.
By mid-November, multiple TikTok videos falsely claimed a 90-day power outage would hit the U.S. on Nov. 17, the fact-checking website PolitiFact reported .
The government of Germany renewed its recommendation for stockpiling at least a three-day supply of such basics as bottled water and non-perishable ready-to-eat food. The photo shows items in an emergency kit from German humanitarian aid organization Malteser Hilfsdienst. (Thilo Schmuelgen/Reuters)
Some events that actually happened likely did little to the quell the paranoia.
A cyberattack raised temperatures in hundreds of supermarket freezers across France in mid-October, spoiling tens of millions of euros worth of food. French authorities blamed Iran-backed hackers .
The U.K. government launched an official "Be Ready" campaign in October, urging the British people to prepare to be self-sufficient for 72 hours in the event of an emergency.
Then just two weeks later, the European Commission unveiled new emergency preparedness guidelines .
Multiple tech outages have Americans asking: Can somebody fix this?
As Europe prepares for the worst, Britons get schooled in preparedness
And then came the cascade of outages that shut down Microsoft services, stranded hundreds of thousands of U.S. air passengers, blocked customers at some U.S. banks from doing transactions online and put the National Security Agency's classified communications network offline all in the space of six days .
Mehdi Hossain, an associate professor of marketing at the University of Rhode Island, has researched the panic buying that defined the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Luggage at San Diego International Airport, three days after the ground-stop order that led to the cancellation of some 20,000 flights across the U.S. (Gregory Bull/The Associated Press)
Hossain says uncertainty over how the pandemic would unfold meant that people had no reference point for how they should prepare, while the high levels of anxiety over the potential seriousness of the threat triggered stockpiling that at times became irrational.
"What was really happening under the hood is the thought that, 'OK, if I don't prepare for this reality, and I suffer and my family suffers because of my lack of preparedness, I am going to regret it,'" Hossain told CBC News.
Trump's team scrambles to calm U.S. fears over tech outages
Flights, banks, emails: What we know about a U.S. wave of tech outages
He says some similar psychology appears to have been at work in recent weeks, fuelled by those false reports on social media.
"It's a snowball kind of effect," Hossain said. "That fake news, when it validates with your fear, you start trusting it more than probably you should, and you start acting on it."
Mike Crawley is a correspondent for CBC News, based in Washington. He began his career as a newspaper reporter in B.C., spent six years as a freelance journalist in various parts of Africa, then joined the CBC in 2005. Mike reported on Ontario politics for 15 years. He was born and raised in Saint John, N.B.
